```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

X <- readRDS(here::here("data", "exclusions_absence.rds"))

INK    <- "#1a1a2e"
PURPLE <- "#361a54"
BRIGHT <- "#993bff"
WARM   <- "#f56300"
BAD    <- "#b2182b"
GREY   <- "#666688"

theme_note <- function(base = 13) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base) +
    theme(
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", colour = PURPLE),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(colour = GREY, size = rel(0.9)),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      axis.title       = element_text(colour = GREY, size = rel(0.9)),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}

# "202526" -> "2025/26", which is how every DfE release labels the year.
yr <- function(x) paste0(substr(x, 1, 4), "/", substr(x, 5, 6))

nat  <- X$national
last <- X$latest_absence
lastx <- X$latest_exclusions
n_now <- nat |> filter(time_period == last)
n_17  <- nat |> filter(time_period == "201617")

excl_row <- X$reasons |> filter(code == "sess_auth_excluded")
ill_row  <- X$reasons |> filter(code == "sess_auth_illness")
un_row   <- X$reasons |> filter(code == "sess_unauth_other")

am <- X$att_models
r2_abs_on_susp  <- am$r2[am$model == "Absence added on top of suspension"]
r2_susp_on_abs  <- am$r2[am$model == "Suspension added on top of absence"]

fe  <- X$abs_models |> filter(spec == "+ school fixed effects")
raw <- X$abs_models |> filter(spec == "Raw")

bh_la <- X$la |> filter(grepl("Brighton and Hove", la_name))
bh    <- X$bh
bh_now <- bh |> filter(time_period == lastx)

fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
ord <- function(n) {
  n <- round(n)
  paste0(n, ifelse(n %% 100 %in% 11:13, "th",
                   c("th","st","nd","rd",rep("th",6))[n %% 10 + 1]))
}
```

::: callout-important
## The question

Brighton & Hove's council has begun asking how exclusions from secondary
schools work in the city. *How to Pull the Right Lever* found that
attendance is the single largest school-level driver of GCSE attainment,
so an interest in exclusions is a reasonable thing to follow from it:
excluded pupils are not in school, and a pupil not in school does not
learn.

The question this note answers is narrower and more useful. **Of the
attendance problem that exists, how much of it is exclusion?** If the
answer is "most of it", exclusions policy is attendance policy and the
council should act. If the answer is "a few per cent", then pressing
schools on exclusions is a cheap substitute for the harder work, and
risks moving the only lever a school fully controls in a direction that
helps nobody.
:::

# The short answer

In `r yr(last)`, across every state-funded secondary school in England:

- Absence ran at **`r fmt(n_now$abs_rate)`%** of possible sessions.
- Sessions missed because a pupil was suspended accounted for
  **`r fmt(excl_row$pp_of_possible, 3)` percentage points** of that —
  **`r fmt(excl_row$pct_of_absence, 1)`% of all absence**.
- Illness accounted for **`r fmt(ill_row$pct_of_absence, 1)`%** and
  unauthorised absence with no given reason for
  **`r fmt(un_row$pct_of_absence, 1)`%**.

If every suspension in England stopped tomorrow and none of those pupils
missed a single further session, the secondary absence rate would fall
from `r fmt(n_now$abs_rate)`% to `r fmt(n_now$abs_rate - excl_row$pp_of_possible)`%.
That is the entire size of the prize, and it is an upper bound rather
than an estimate, because it assumes a pupil who is no longer suspended
attends perfectly instead.

::: callout-note
## Verdict

**Exclusions are a real but small part of the attendance story, and
they are a symptom of it rather than a cause of it.**

They are not a red herring — the association between a school's
suspension rate and its attendance is strong and worth understanding.
But the association runs overwhelmingly through *the same pupils*,
not through the suspensions themselves: schools that suspend more have
more absence of **every** kind, including the kinds suspension cannot
touch. Treating exclusions as the attendance lever would be acting on
the symptom that is easiest to count and easiest to blame a school for.

For Brighton & Hove specifically the case is weaker still. The city
suspends **less** than most of England and has close to the **worst**
attendance in the country. Whatever is driving absence here, it is not
how often the schools suspend.
:::

# What the data is

Three published sources, all Open Government Licence v3.0, assembled by
[`R/15_exclusions.R`](https://github.com/adamdennett/school_attainment_tool/blob/main/R/15_exclusions.R).

```{r tbl-sources}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Source, ~`What it gives`, ~Coverage,
  "Pupil absence in schools in England (school level, autumn + spring)",
  "Sessions missed, split by register code — including code E, *excluded, no alternative provision made*",
  paste0("2016/17 to ", yr(last)),
  "Suspensions and permanent exclusions in England (school level)",
  "Headcount, suspensions, permanent exclusions, and pupils receiving one or more suspension",
  paste0("2006/07 to ", yr(lastx)),
  "This project's school characteristics panel",
  "Attainment 8, disadvantage, EAL, SEN and full-year absence, as used throughout *Pulling the Right Lever*",
  paste0(yr(min(X$panel_years)), " to ", yr(max(X$panel_years)))
) |> knitr::kable()
```

Three things about this are worth saying plainly before any number is
quoted.

**Absence here is autumn and spring terms only.** That is the basis the
DfE publishes early enough to reach `r yr(last)`, and it is the basis
used in the `r yr(last)` addendum to the main report, so the two agree.
Summer-term absence is excluded for every year equally.

**The exclusions collection runs a year behind.** Suspensions for
`r yr(last)` are not published until summer 2027. Everything joining
exclusions to absence therefore stops at `r yr(lastx)`; the absence
decomposition alone runs to `r yr(last)`.

**Code E is measured from the attendance register, not inferred.** The
central number in this note — how many sessions suspension actually
costs — is not derived by multiplying suspensions by an assumed length.
It is a column in the published absence file, counted by schools as they
mark the register. `r fmt(X$national$schools[X$national$time_period == last], 0)`
secondary schools report it.

# How big is exclusion, as a share of absence?

## Every reason, ranked

```{r fig-reasons}
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Secondary absence in England by register code, ", yr(last), ", autumn and spring terms. Code E — suspension — is highlighted.")'
d <- X$reasons |>
  filter(sessions > 0) |>
  mutate(reason = factor(reason, levels = rev(reason)),
         is_e = code == "sess_auth_excluded")

ggplot(d, aes(reason, pct_of_absence, fill = is_e)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", pct_of_absence)),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3.4, colour = INK) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = BAD, "FALSE" = "#c7bbd8"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.13)),
                     labels = label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of all absent sessions",
       title = "Suspension is the eighth-largest reason a secondary pupil is absent",
       subtitle = paste0("England, state-funded secondary, ", yr(last),
                         ". Illness alone is ",
                         round(ill_row$pct_of_absence / excl_row$pct_of_absence),
                         " times larger than suspension.")) +
  theme_note(12)
```

Illness is the mountain. "Unauthorised, other" — the code that carries
most persistent absence — is the second mountain. Suspension is the
`r ord(which(X$reasons$code == "sess_auth_excluded"))` largest reason a
secondary pupil in England is not in a lesson, behind being late and
behind unauthorised family holidays.

## And it has grown

```{r fig-trend}
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-cap: "Suspension's contribution to secondary absence, England, autumn and spring terms. Left: as a share of all absence. Right: in percentage points of possible sessions. 2019/20 is absent from the published series."
p <- nat |> mutate(year = yr(time_period))

g1 <- ggplot(p, aes(year, excl_share_of_abs, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(colour = BAD, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(colour = BAD, size = 2.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), labels = label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Share of all absence") +
  theme_note(11) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

g2 <- ggplot(p, aes(year, excl_pp, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(colour = BAD, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(colour = BAD, size = 2.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Percentage points of possible sessions") +
  theme_note(11) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

patchwork::wrap_plots(g1, g2) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(
    title = "Exclusion absence has roughly doubled since 2016/17 — from a very low base",
    theme = theme_note(12))
```

This is the honest part of the case for taking exclusions seriously.
Suspension's contribution to absence has gone from
`r fmt(n_17$excl_pp, 3)` percentage points in 2016/17 to
`r fmt(n_now$excl_pp, 3)` in `r yr(last)`, and England's suspension rate
has risen from `r fmt(bh$susp_rate_eng[bh$time_period == "201617"], 1)`
per 100 pupils to `r fmt(bh$susp_rate_eng[bh$time_period == lastx], 1)`.
Something real is happening in school behaviour policy.

But the scale has not changed. Doubling a figure that was
`r fmt(n_17$excl_share_of_abs, 1)`% of absence gets you to
`r fmt(n_now$excl_share_of_abs, 1)`% of absence.

## And nationally, it has risen while attendance improved

```{r fig-divergence}
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Suspension rate against persistent absence, England secondary, indexed to 2021/22 = 100. The exclusions series stops a year earlier than absence."
idx <- bh |>
  select(time_period, susp = susp_rate_eng, pa = pa_rate_eng) |>
  filter(time_period >= "202122") |>
  mutate(across(c(susp, pa), ~100 * .x / .x[time_period == "202122"])) |>
  pivot_longer(c(susp, pa), names_to = "series", values_to = "idx") |>
  mutate(series = recode(series,
                         susp = "Suspension rate",
                         pa = "Persistent absence"),
         year = yr(time_period))

ggplot(idx, aes(year, idx, colour = series, group = series)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "31", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Suspension rate" = BAD,
                                 "Persistent absence" = "#2166ac")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Index, 2021/22 = 100", colour = NULL,
       title = "Since 2021/22, suspensions rose by half while persistent absence fell by a fifth",
       subtitle = "If suspension were driving the attendance crisis, these two lines would move together.") +
  theme_note(12) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Over the four years for which both series exist, England's secondary
suspension rate rose by about half while persistent absence fell by
about a fifth. That is not proof that suspensions do not matter — both
series are moved by other things, and the post-COVID attendance recovery
is doing most of the work on the blue line. But it is the opposite of
what you would see if exclusions were the engine of the attendance
problem, and anyone proposing that they are has to account for it.

# Does a school that suspends more have worse attendance?

Yes, strongly. This is the finding that makes the council's interest
reasonable, and it deserves to be stated at full strength before it is
taken apart.

```{r fig-scatter}
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Every state-funded secondary school in England with at least 100 on roll, ", yr(lastx), ". Left: headline absence. Right: absence with every suspension session removed.")'
s <- X$joined |>
  filter(time_period == lastx, !is.na(susp_rate), susp_rate > 0) |>
  mutate(bh = grepl("Brighton and Hove", la_name))

sc <- function(yv, ylab, ttl) {
  r <- cor(s$susp_rate, s[[yv]], use = "complete")
  ggplot(s, aes(susp_rate, .data[[yv]])) +
    geom_point(colour = "#b9a7ce", alpha = 0.35, size = 0.9) +
    geom_point(data = filter(s, bh), colour = BAD, size = 2.1) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
                colour = PURPLE, linewidth = 0.9, linetype = "22") +
    scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10",
                       breaks = c(1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300)) +
    labs(x = "Suspensions per 100 pupils (log scale)", y = ylab,
         title = ttl, subtitle = sprintf("r = %+.2f", r)) +
    theme_note(11)
}

patchwork::wrap_plots(
  sc("abs_rate", "Absence rate (%)", "All absence"),
  sc("abs_ex_excl", "Absence rate (%)", "Absence excluding suspension sessions")) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(
    title = "Schools that suspend more have more absence — of every kind, not just the kind suspension causes",
    subtitle = "Brighton & Hove's ten secondary schools in red.",
    theme = theme_note(12))
```

The right-hand panel is the whole argument. It removes every single
session that a suspension caused, and the relationship barely moves:
from r = `r sprintf("%+.2f", cor(s$susp_rate, s$abs_rate, use = "complete"))`
to r = `r sprintf("%+.2f", cor(s$susp_rate, s$abs_ex_excl, use = "complete"))`.

A school that suspends a lot is a school where a lot of pupils are
absent for reasons that have nothing to do with being suspended. The
suspension rate is **telling you about the pupils, not doing something
to them**.

## What survives a control for intake

```{r tbl-models}
X$abs_models |>
  transmute(
    Specification = spec,
    `Extra absence per suspension per 100 pupils (pp)` = sprintf("%+.4f", beta),
    `t` = sprintf("%.0f", t),
    `R²` = sprintf("%.3f", r2),
    `School-years` = format(n, big.mark = ",")) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

Each row adds a control. The outcome throughout is **absence with
suspension sessions already removed**, so nothing here is mechanical.

The last row is the one that matters. It carries a separate intercept
for every school, so it no longer compares a school in Blackpool with a
school in Surrey. It asks: when a school suspends more *than it usually
does*, does it also have worse attendance *than it usually does*? That
differences away everything fixed about the intake, the catchment, the
building and the leadership.

The answer is yes, and it is **`r fmt(fe$beta / raw$beta * 100, 0)`% the
size of the raw association**. `r fmt(round(100 * (1 - fe$beta / raw$beta)), 0)`%
of what the scatter plot shows is schools being different from each
other, not suspension doing anything.

::: callout-tip
## What that coefficient means in practice

A school that raises its suspension rate by 10 per 100 pupils — a large
move, well beyond what most schools do in a year — is associated with
**`r fmt(fe$beta * 10, 2)` percentage points** more non-suspension
absence. Against a mean absence rate of around `r fmt(n_now$abs_rate, 1)`%.

And even that is an association, not an effect. The plausible mechanism
runs the other way: a pupil who has disengaged both stops attending and
gets suspended, and a school whose cohort is unravelling does more of
both in the same year.
:::

# Does any of this reach attainment?

This is the step the council's theory needs. *Pulling the Right Lever*
established that absence is the largest school-level predictor of GCSE
attainment. If exclusions matter to attainment, they should add
something to that model.

```{r tbl-att}
X$att_models |>
  mutate(model = recode(model,
    "Intake only" = "Intake only (disadvantage, EAL)",
    "+ absence" = "Intake + absence",
    "+ suspension rate" = "Intake + suspension rate",
    "+ both" = "Intake + absence + suspension rate")) |>
  transmute(Model = model, `R²` = sprintf("%.4f", r2),
            `School-years` = format(n, big.mark = ",")) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrr")
```

Read the last two rows as the test:

- Starting from a model that already has the suspension rate in it,
  **adding absence raises R² by `r fmt(r2_abs_on_susp, 3)`**.
- Starting from a model that already has absence in it, **adding the
  suspension rate raises R² by `r fmt(r2_susp_on_abs, 3)`**.

Absence does about **`r fmt(r2_abs_on_susp / r2_susp_on_abs, 0)` times as
much work** as suspension in explaining what a school's cohort gets at
GCSE. Suspension is not worthless — the coefficient is negative and
statistically significant on 12,000-odd school-years, as almost anything
is at that sample size — but once you know a school's absence rate,
knowing how often it suspends tells you very nearly nothing further.

# Brighton & Hove

## The city suspends below average and attends near the bottom

```{r fig-la}
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Local authorities with more than 2,000 secondary pupils, ", yr(lastx), ". Brighton & Hove in red.")'
la <- X$la |> mutate(bh = grepl("Brighton and Hove", la_name))

ggplot(la, aes(susp_rate, abs_rate)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#b9a7ce", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = PURPLE, linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "22") +
  geom_point(data = filter(la, bh), colour = BAD, size = 3.6) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = filter(la, bh), aes(label = la_name),
                           colour = BAD, fontface = "bold", size = 4,
                           nudge_y = 0.5, nudge_x = 6) +
  labs(x = "Suspensions per 100 secondary pupils",
       y = "Absence rate (%)",
       title = "Brighton & Hove: among the lowest suspenders, among the worst attenders",
       subtitle = sprintf(
         "%.0f of %d local authorities suspend more than Brighton & Hove. Only %.0f have worse attendance.",
         bh_la$rank_susp - 1, bh_la$n_la, bh_la$rank_abs - 1)) +
  theme_note(12)
```

This is the finding that should settle the question locally.

Brighton & Hove is the **`r ord(bh_la$rank_abs)` worst** of
`r bh_la$n_la` local authorities for secondary absence, at
`r fmt(bh_la$abs_rate)`% against an England figure of
`r fmt(bh_now$abs_rate_eng)`%. On suspensions it ranks
**`r ord(bh_la$rank_susp)`** — meaning `r bh_la$rank_susp - 1` local
authorities suspend *more* than it does, and it sits comfortably in the
lower half of the country at `r fmt(bh_la$susp_rate, 1)` suspensions per
100 pupils against England's `r fmt(bh_now$susp_rate_eng, 1)`.

Exclusion sessions account for `r fmt(bh_la$excl_pp, 3)` percentage
points of the city's `r fmt(bh_la$abs_rate)`% absence rate — about
**`r fmt(100 * bh_la$excl_pp / bh_la$abs_rate, 1)`% of it**, lower than
the national share of `r fmt(n_now$excl_share_of_abs, 1)`%.

A city that suspends less than most of England and attends worse than
almost all of it does not have an exclusions-driven attendance problem.
It has an attendance problem.

## Permanent exclusion is close to extinct here

```{r tbl-bh}
bh |>
  transmute(Year = yr(time_period),
            `Suspensions per 100` = sprintf("%.1f", susp_rate_bh),
            `England` = sprintf("%.1f", susp_rate_eng),
            `Permanent exclusions` = perm_bh,
            `Absence (%)` = sprintf("%.2f", abs_rate_bh),
            `England ` = sprintf("%.2f", abs_rate_eng),
            `of which suspension (pp)` = sprintf("%.3f", excl_pp_bh),
            `Persistent absence (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", pa_rate_bh)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrrrr")
```

Across ten secondary schools and roughly
`r format(round(bh_la$headcount, -2), big.mark = ",")` pupils, the city
permanently excluded `r bh$perm_bh[bh$time_period == "201617"]` children
in 2016/17, `r bh$perm_bh[bh$time_period == "202122"]` in 2021/22, none
at all in 2023/24, and `r bh$perm_bh[bh$time_period == lastx]` in
`r yr(lastx)`. Whatever problem the city has, it is not that its schools
are permanently excluding children.

Note also the direction of travel. Between 2021/22 and `r yr(lastx)` the
city's suspension rate rose from `r fmt(bh$susp_rate_bh[bh$time_period == "202122"], 1)`
to `r fmt(bh_now$susp_rate_bh, 1)` per 100 — and its persistent absence
*fell*, from `r fmt(bh$pa_rate_bh[bh$time_period == "202122"], 1)`% to
`r fmt(bh_now$pa_rate_bh, 1)`%. The two moved in opposite directions,
here as nationally.

## School by school

```{r tbl-bh-schools}
X$bh_schools |>
  filter(time_period == lastx) |>
  arrange(desc(susp_rate)) |>
  transmute(School = sub(" (School|Catholic School|High School|Community Academy|School and Sixth Form Centre)$", "", school_name),
            `On roll` = format(round(headcount), big.mark = ","),
            `Susp. per 100` = sprintf("%.1f", susp_rate),
            `Pupils suspended (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", one_plus_susp_rate),
            `Perm. excl.` = perm_excl,
            `Absence (%)` = sprintf("%.2f", abs_rate),
            `of which susp. (pp)` = sprintf("%.2f", excl_pp),
            `Persistent absence (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", pa_rate),
            `Attainment 8` = sprintf("%.1f", att8)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrrrrr")
```

Three things stand out, and all three argue the same way.

**Longhill is the one school where the mechanical effect is visible at
all.** It suspends far more than any other school in the city, and
suspension costs it
`r fmt(X$bh_schools$excl_pp[X$bh_schools$time_period == lastx & grepl("Longhill", X$bh_schools$school_name)], 2)`
percentage points of attendance. Against an absence rate of
`r fmt(X$bh_schools$abs_rate[X$bh_schools$time_period == lastx & grepl("Longhill", X$bh_schools$school_name)], 1)`%
and persistent absence at
`r fmt(X$bh_schools$pa_rate[X$bh_schools$time_period == lastx & grepl("Longhill", X$bh_schools$school_name)], 0)`%
of its pupils. Even at the city's extreme, suspension is about
`r fmt(100 * X$bh_schools$excl_pp[X$bh_schools$time_period == lastx & grepl("Longhill", X$bh_schools$school_name)] / X$bh_schools$abs_rate[X$bh_schools$time_period == lastx & grepl("Longhill", X$bh_schools$school_name)], 0)`%
of the problem.

**Brighton Aldridge suspends below the city average and has the city's
second-worst attendance.** Its persistent absence is
`r fmt(X$bh_schools$pa_rate[X$bh_schools$time_period == lastx & grepl("^Brighton Aldridge", X$bh_schools$school_name)], 0)`%
of pupils on a suspension rate of
`r fmt(X$bh_schools$susp_rate[X$bh_schools$time_period == lastx & grepl("^Brighton Aldridge", X$bh_schools$school_name)], 1)`
per 100 — a seventh of Longhill's. The school with the best value added in
the city, serving the most disadvantaged intake, is not solving its
attendance problem by suspending, and is not causing it by suspending
either.

**Patcham reports zero suspensions, four years running.** On a roll of
about
`r format(round(X$bh_schools$headcount[X$bh_schools$time_period == lastx & grepl("Patcham", X$bh_schools$school_name)], -1), big.mark = ",")`,
in a school that recorded 193 suspensions in 2006/07. Four consecutive
exact zeros is unusual enough that it may reflect recording practice as
much as policy, and it would be worth the council asking — but taken at
face value it is the cleanest possible test of the theory, and Patcham's
absence rate of
`r fmt(X$bh_schools$abs_rate[X$bh_schools$time_period == lastx & grepl("Patcham", X$bh_schools$school_name)], 1)`%
is good for the city without being exceptional.

# What this does not show

Four honest limits, because the finding is only useful if it survives
them.

**This is about suspension, not about the children suspended.** The
claim here is about aggregates: suspension is a small share of total
absence. For an individual child who is suspended repeatedly, the
disruption is serious, the association with poor outcomes is severe, and
nothing in this note argues otherwise. A policy aimed at the few hundred
children in this city with repeat suspensions can be worth doing on its
own merits while being irrelevant to the city's attendance rate.

**Permanent exclusion does not appear in a school's absence at all.**
A permanently excluded pupil comes off the roll, so their subsequent
absence belongs to alternative provision or to the next school. The
figures above therefore understate exclusion's total effect on
attendance in the system — but permanent exclusion is running at
`r bh$perm_bh[bh$time_period == lastx]` child a year across the whole of
secondary Brighton & Hove, so the understatement is not large here.

**Nor do off-rolling or managed moves.** A pupil moved off a roll
informally leaves no trace in either dataset. If the council's real
interest is in that, exclusions data is not where it will be found, and
the school-level absence data will not find it either. This is a genuine
gap and it is the one question in this area where the published data
cannot answer the council.

**None of the models here identify a causal effect.** They establish
that the association between suspension and non-suspension absence
survives controls and shrinks dramatically under school fixed effects.
They cannot rule out that some of what remains is causal. What they do
rule out is that it is *large*.

# What would be more use

If the council's underlying concern is attendance — and on the evidence
of *Pulling the Right Lever* it should be — then the published data
points somewhere else entirely.

`r fmt(ill_row$pct_of_absence, 1)`% of secondary absence is illness and
`r fmt(un_row$pct_of_absence, 1)`% is unauthorised with no given reason.
Between them they are
`r fmt(ill_row$pct_of_absence + un_row$pct_of_absence, 0)`% of the
problem. Persistent absence in Brighton & Hove sits at
`r fmt(bh_now$pa_rate_bh, 1)`% of secondary pupils — more than one child
in four missing at least a tenth of their schooling.

Three questions the same data could answer, and which nobody has asked:

1. **Which children?** Persistent absence is heavily concentrated. A
   pupil-level view the council already holds would say whether the same
   children are persistently absent year on year, and what else is true
   of them.
2. **How far do they travel?** The city's school system work shows
   disadvantaged children in Brighton & Hove travel further than their
   classmates, and longer journeys are associated with lower attendance.
   That is a lever the council controls directly, through catchments
   and admissions, and it has never been costed against attendance.
3. **What happens to attendance after a suspension?** The data to answer
   this is in the council's own attendance returns, not in any DfE
   publication. If suspension really does start a spiral, that is where
   it would show up — and it would be a far better argument than the
   aggregate one.

::: callout-important
## The one-line answer

Exclusions matter to the children they happen to, and they are worth
understanding on their own terms. As an explanation of Brighton &
Hove's attendance problem, they are **about
`r fmt(100 * bh_la$excl_pp / bh_la$abs_rate, 0)`% of it** — in a city
that already suspends less than three-quarters of England while
attending worse than all but `r bh_la$rank_abs - 1` local authorities in
it.

If the city wants attendance to improve, exclusions are not where the
work is.
:::
